Govt weighs NFC-based financial framework for Gilgit-Baltistan. GILGIT: Federal Minister for Law and Justice Senator Azam Nazeer Tarar said on Friday that consultations on the constitutional and legal status of Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) were under way, while the federal government was considering an arrangement to give the region a share in the National Finance Commission (NFC) award. The federal government currently provides annual financial grants to GB, while successive governments in the region have demanded a share in the NFC award. The federal minister said broad consultations would be held on GB’s future administrative and constitutional arrangement and all relevant stakeholders would be taken on board. According to the Ministry of Law and Jus­tice, Senator Tarar invited GB Chief Minister Amjad Hussain Advocate and Leader of the Opposition Hafiz Hafeezur Rehman to the next meeting of the GB Issues Working Group. GB Assembly backs AJK-style arrangement after CM gets cabinet approval The meeting, chaired by Senator Tarar, was attended by officials from GB, the ministries of defence, foreign affairs, and Kashmir Affairs and GB, as well as the GB Council. It discussed constitutional, legal, financial and administrative issues and reviewed previous reports, possible constitutional options and proposals for strengthening GB’s financial resources. Participants also examined practical reforms within the existing governance framework. Senator Tarar directed the working group to formulate practical proposals and prepare an interim report, along with recommendations, for the main committee. He said more time would be required to reach an agreed constitutional and legal solution, stressing that national consensus was essential. Protecting the rights of GB’s people and ensuring their sense of equality, he added, remained a priority. AJK-style arrangement Meanwhile, the GB Assembly unanimously approved a proposed financial agreement between the federal and GB governments, modelled on the financial arrangement between the federal government and Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK). Chief Minister Amjad Hussain Advocate moved the proposal in the assembly on Friday. The GB cabinet had already approved it. The chief minister said the GB government had sought federal assistance to address its budget deficit and that a committee constituted by the Prime Minister’s Office had subsequently examined a mechanism for providing the region a share in the NFC. He said the federal finance division had raised an objection that GB could become a member of the NFC only after a constitutional amendment because the region was not a constitutional part of Pakistan. As a result, he said, an NFC arrangement could not be established before such an amendment. The finance division had suggested that, until then, GB could adopt an arrangement similar to the one in place for AJK, subject to approval by the GB Assembly and adoption by the federal government. The arrangement would remain in force until GB became a constitutional part of Pak­istan and was included in the NFC, he said. The chief minister said GB faced a financial shortfall of around Rs17 billion against its estimated requirement of Rs320bn. Under the proposed agreement, the federal government would provide Rs250bn to the region. He expressed hope that the arrangement would help meet GB’s financial requirements, improve its overall financial position and provide greater stability. “If both options are not adopted, instead of providing Rs45bn, you would be providing only around Rs100bn under the existing model,” he said. He said the AJK-style agreement should be conditional on the eventual amendment of the Constitution and GB’s inclusion in the NFC. The house unanimously approved the proposal. PM’s committee examining NFC framework Chief Minister Amjad Hussain had met Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in July after assuming office and demanded a greater financial share for GB. An official told Dawn that the prime minister subsequently constituted a high-level committee, chaired by Federal Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives Ahsan Iqbal, to examine key financial, governance and development issues concerning the region. The committee has reviewed GB’s long-term financial sustainability, hydropower development, power-sector reforms, climate resilience, digital connectivity, public service delivery and development priorities. According to the official, a key focus is developing a transparent resource-sharing mechanism based on NFC principles to ensure fair and predictable fiscal transfers to GB. The committee is expected to propose an NFC-based financial framework. Published in Dawn, September 12th, 2026

Yemen flare-up. INTENSE fighting has broken out between the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, and the pro-Iran Houthi Ansarallah group that currently holds the capital Sanaa and much of the north. While the hostilities will add to the miseries of the Yemeni people, the conflict is tied to the US-Iran war as well. Questions have also been raised about the involvement of Saudi Arabia’s allies, including Pakistan, as the Houthis have struck positions in the kingdom . The Yemeni front was largely quiet since the 2022 Saudi-Houthi ceasefire took effect. But over the past few weeks, there has been open war between the government and Ansarallah. In fact, the Houthis have captured the strategically important city of Mocha as well as key islands off the coast, leaving them largely in control of who gets to pass through the Bab al-Mandeb strait. The Houthis say maritime passage is open to all except Saudi vessels. As the Yemeni front heats up, it is welcome that Pakistan has taken a measured approach to the conflict, in light of its recently upgraded defence ties with Saudi Arabia . In a statement , the Foreign Office said that while Pakistan offered “unwavering support” for Saudi Arabia, there were no plans to join the kingdom in striking the Houthis. The FO further added that Pakistan was “desirous of peace and stability in Yemen”. This is a balanced stance on what is geopolitically a very tricky issue. While Pakistan has indeed signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, it would be a risky endeavour to join offensive action against forces in a third country. Instead, Pakistan should push for an immediate ceasefire and a diplomatic solution to the Yemeni conflict. While Iran has influence over the Houthis, the Yemeni armed group makes its own decisions. However, Islamabad can use its diplomatic channels with Tehran to ask the latter to convince the Houthis to pursue a diplomatic solution. The Yemeni group should halt its attacks on Saudi Arabia; the kingdom, too, should refrain from targeting Yemen. Moreover, Ansarallah has demanded an end to the blockade of Yemen. If Riyadh were to agree to this, it would send a positive message to the pro-Iran group, and could help restart talks for a long-term peace. The fact is that if there is to be a sustainable solution to the Yemeni conflict, then a power-sharing agreement including all of Yemen’s tribes and sects is needed. If the conflict escalates, Bab al-Mandeb could face a blockade just as the Strait of Hormuz does. This would spell more trouble for the global economy. Therefore, Pakistan and regional states need to push for a ceasefire and peace talks involving the Houthis, the Saudis and the Yemeni government. Published in Dawn, September 12th, 2026

The Google bargain. GOOGLE’S new local office gave the government a week to celebrate. It was inaugurated at the Prime Minister’s House, where Pakistan and Google signed an MoU three days later . Pakistani students will receive free access to Google AI Plus and Gemini for a year, while Google is targeting 150,000 career certificates in 2026. The two sides will cooperate on an AI Centre of Excellence in Islamabad. These commitments build on a Chromebook assembly line launched with local partners in Haripur in 2025. Google.org has also committed $500,000 to Digital Pasban, which aims to reach 200,000 households with Urdu safety material and workshops. This is welcome. International technology companies can create jobs, train people and support local developers. But the important question is how this relationship will take shape. The agreement also mentions AI analytics for the Federal Board of Revenue, agriculture, digital payments, and public services. These are no longer workshops or subscriptions. They reach into state machinery and involve data about how citizens earn, spend, own property, and interact with government. This is where celebration must give way to policy. The government should assess this partnership against five questions: whether it builds national capacity, offers fair economic terms, keeps public data under Pakistani control, protects critical datasets, and guarantees citizens enforceable privacy rights. The government should assess the partnership with Google against five questions. The first is whether free access builds capacity or dependence. A year of Gemini may teach students to use an AI tool, but it will not give universities shared GPU clusters, enable local firms to host sensitive workloads, or help researchers build models around Pakistani languages. Chromebook assembly may create jobs, but it is not necessarily technology transfer. The government should ask what capabilities Pakistani firms will acquire and how much value will remain here. The second question concerns the economic bargain. Google and Meta take a dominant share of Pakistan’s digital advertising market, with one estimate placing their combined share above 85 per cent. Local publishers and advertising firms are left competing for a much smaller share. Pakistan enacted a 5pc tax on the gross proceeds of certain foreign digital suppliers in 2025. Google was reportedly told that its local presence placed it outside the tax. The government later withdrew the tax for all covered foreign suppliers following objections from American business groups. A punitive tax would be self-defeating, but Pakistan is a large market and should negotiate accordingly. Local presence should bring fair taxation, skilled employment, local procurement, technology transfer, and reinvestment. An office and training targets cannot substitute for an equitable economic bargain. The third question is who controls public data and benefits from it. There is no public evidence that Google has received Pakistani government datasets. Its standard Cloud terms state that customer data will not be used to train or fine-tune AI models without prior permission. That is reassuring, but it does not tell us what safeguards govern this partnership. The government has published summaries of the MoU, but not its full text, and has not explained what data may be shared, where it will be stored, who may access it, or whether it may be used to improve a model. These conditions cannot be left to private contracts beyond public scrutiny. Data produced by Pakistani citizens and institutions is a national asset. Giving a global company access without clear limits could allow value created in Pakistan to strengthen systems owned elsewhere, while Pakistan remains their customer. There is an uncomfortable historical analogy here. The East India Company entered South Asia as a commercial enterprise, but gradually extracted the region’s resources and accumulated power over its markets. Big Tech companies do not govern territory, but their business model can produce a modern form of extraction. They take revenue, attention, and data from large populations, use them to strengthen systems owned elsewhere, and often return little in the form of local infrastructure or technological ownership. Pakistan should welcome investment, but it should not mistake access to foreign technology for control over its own digital future. The fourth question concerns critical information. Criminal records, tax histories, biometric information, law-enforcement databases and defence-related material cannot be treated like ordinary data. Google Public Sector received a contract with a ceiling of $200 million from the US Department of Defence in 2025. The Pentagon has since announced agreements to deploy AI developed by Google and other companies on classified networks. This does not mean that Google will misuse Pakistani data, but dependence on a company integrated into another country’s defence infrastructure raises national security questions. Access to critical datasets should be restricted by law and subject to independent security review, strict controls and clear rules on storage and deletion. More broadly, Pakistan should avoid becoming overly reliant on foreign systems. The fifth question is whether Pakistanis will have enforceable rights over their information. Pakistan still has no comprehensive personal data protection statute in force. A credible law must bind companies and the state, establish an independent regulator, require purpose limitation and data minimisation, and provide remedies. Meta’s €1.2 billion European privacy penalty over transfers of user data to the US shows why enforcement matters. Such a law should also draw on Helen Nissenbaum’s theory of contextual integrity, which holds that privacy depends on whether information flows are appropriate to the context in which the data was provided. Tax data should not become AI training material, and a police complaint should not feed an unrelated predictive tool without clear legal authority and safeguards. Google’s presence can be valuable, but one company cannot revolutionise Pakistan’s digital economy. Nor can borrowed infrastructure provide the independence on which a genuine digital economy must rest. The government should publish the MoU, disclose Google’s tax treatment and protect sensitive datasets through law and auditable contracts. At the same time, Pakistan must invest in power, sovereign compute, local data centres, Pakistani language models, universities and public digital infrastructure. Google can contribute to that ecosystem, but it cannot become the ecosystem. Otherwise, Pakistan will gain access to the future while ensuring that someone else continues to own it. The writer is the founder of Media Matters for Democracy. Published in Dawn, September 12th, 2026

More than a single day. “No man is an island, entire of itself; … any man’s death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind; and therefore, never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.” JOHN Donne wrote these words four centuries ago, and Ernest Hemingway later used a part of the quote as the title of his novel. The quote describes a principle that modern epidemiology has since validated with data: that no death by suicide is a purely private event. Each death reverberates through a family, a workplace, a community, and, in aggregate, through the statistical and narrative record of a nation’s health. Every year, on Sept 10, the world observes International Suicide Prevention Day, and every year I find myself uneasy with the framing of this ‘observance’. In practice, it so often slides towards something that resembles a commemoration where panels are convened, experts invited, and statistics projected onto screens. The day then passes and is folded back into the calendar — until it comes around again the following year. I do not begrudge any of this; awareness, conversations, panels and specifically data, matter. My unease is narrower and rests in the belief that suicide is not a subject that can be adequately held by a single day, however earnestly it is marked. It is a chronic and distributed public health problem that requires sustained clinical, social, and policy attention throughout the year. The task is to find and reinforce the one thread that tethers the struggling individual to hope. As a physician, I practise under an oath that obliges me to preserve life and relieve suffering, grounded in the biological premise that human beings possess an innate desire to survive. This means that if you are a living creature, you must want to live. This is not simply an ethical assumption; it is observable at a physiological level, in the autonomic responses that mobilise the body against threat and injury. When a patient reaches the point of ending their own life, the clinical interpretation is not that they have uncovered some previously hidden preference for non-existence. Suicidal ideation is clinically read as evidence that they have reached the outer edge of despair, a point at which an underlying and usually treatable condition, often a brain illness like depression, psychoses, substance abuse or something else, has temporarily overwhelmed that baseline instinct to live. Our task, in that moment, is not to argue someone out of their pain, but to identify and reinforce that one thread, however thin, that tethers them to hope and life — long enough for treatment to take effect. Within medicine we often draw an analogy between suicidal crisis and other acute, potentially fatal medical events, such as cardiac arrest, an ischemic stroke, or pulmonary embolism. This comparison is not made lightly. It reflects a genuine clinical understanding that such crises are frequently time-limited, and that patients who receive timely and appropriate care — whether hospitalisation, medication, psychotherapy, or structured follow-up — very often go on to recover and to build lives they later describe as worth living. Understood this way, suicide prevention is less a philosophical argument against a person’s stated wish to die and more a form of emergency medicine: stabilise the acute crisis first, and treat the underlying condition once the immediate danger has passed. And yet, even while holding that conviction firmly, the framework does not fully resolve a question I continue to face in clinical practice. When a terminally ill patient signs a do-not-resuscitate order, declining further intervention as their body finally fails, it is generally regarded as a legitimate exercise of patient autonomy. The ethical basis for distinguishing that decision though, from a decision to end one’s life in the context of prolonged, treatment-resistant psychological suffering is less clear than clinical convention often assumes. At what point does a physician’s judgement that a patient ‘lacks the capacity’ to make such a decision become a form of paternalism rather than clinical care? I do not raise this to suggest that suicide should be approached with anything other than urgent clinical concern; the evidence for the treatability of most suicidal crises is strong, and that evidence should govern practice. I raise it because intellectual honesty requires acknowledging the limits of our current ethical frameworks, and enduring the discomfort of the question, rather than rushing to resolve the tension to avoid facing it. Even so, the clinical and philosophical dimensions of this issue address only part of the picture, because suicide is not solely an individual pathology; it is also a measurable outcome of the socioeconomic conditions in which individuals live. This is particularly relevant to the population now coming of age, and which is confronting a convergence of structural pressures with limited precedent: climate instability, economic contraction, political volatility, widening income inequality, and, more recently, uncertainty about labour market disruption from automation and artificial intelligence. These conditions have not been matched by a corresponding adjustment in social expectations. Academic achievement, career stability, and conventional markers of success remain the default benchmarks, even as the institutional infrastructure that once made those benchmarks attainable has weakened. This mismatch between expectation and structural opportunity is a documented risk factor and a significant contributor to the hopelessness that so often precedes suicidal thinking. Given all of this, a more honest and accurate framing of the annual suicide prevention day is to treat it as an invitation to structured, sustained and evidence-based reflection, individually, clinically, and at the level of policy, on why a species biologically oriented towards survival and social connection continues, in significant and rising numbers, to arrive at a decision to end its own life. That question cannot be resolved within a single day, a single panel discussion, or a single article. It is a question owed, on a continuing basis, to every person currently at risk. Donne’s observation that the bell tolls for all of us remains, four centuries later, an accurate description of what’s at stake. The writer is a consultant child, adolescent and adult psychiatrist and founder & CEO at Synapse Pakistan Neuroscience Institute. Sikh pilgrims in Faisalabad stopped from flying to India over incomplete documents. LAHORE: Around 100 Pakistani Sikh pilgrims, including women and children, were stopped at Faisalabad International Airport on Friday from travelling to India to perform religious rituals at Gurdwara Sri Hemkund Sahib, after the immigration authorities raised questions over their travel documents and arrangements. The pilgrims, who had secured Indian visas independently, arrived at the airport to board a Gulf-bound flight for onward travel to India. However, immigration officials prevented them from proceeding, citing the absence of return tickets and a no objection certificate (NOC) from the relevant federal ministry, according to a senior Punjab government official. The official told Dawn that the pilgrims had obtained their Indian visas without involving the Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (PSGPC) or the Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETPB), the bodies generally associated with facilitating Sikh pilgrimage-related travel. “Interestingly, they opted to travel to India through the Gulf rather than using the Wagah border,” the official said. Authorities say they didn’t have return tickets and lacked NOC from ministry Pakistan and India currently have no direct air, rail or regular road travel link, making pilgrimage journeys particularly complicated. The pilgrims had, therefore, planned to reach India through an indirect air route. The situation at the airport triggered distress among the pilgrims, with videos circulating on social media showing Sikh passengers appealing to the authorities to allow them to proceed. In one video, a Pakistani Sikh said the group had been waiting at the airport for around four hours after being stopped by immigration officials. “We have been languishing at the Faisalabad airport for the last four hours. Someone should take notice of our plight and help us proceed to our destination,” he said. Another affected pilgrim made an emotional appeal to the government, urging it to allow the group to travel to India so that they could perform their religious obligations at the sacred Sikh shrine. Gurdwara Sri Hemkund Sahib, located in Chamoli district of Uttarakhand, is one of the most revered Sikh pilgrimage sites in India. The shrine is associated with Guru Gobind Singh, the 10th Sikh Guru. An official source told Dawn that the government had taken notice of the matter and was considering allowing the pilgrims to travel to India via the Wagah border. The development comes at a time when religious travel between Pakistan and India remains subject to heightened scrutiny and complicated procedures because of the absence of normal bilateral transport links. (Tariq Saeed From Toba Tek Singh also contributed to this report) Published in Dawn, September 12th, 2026

Saudi Arabia says Iraqi drones forced temporary closure of crucial oil pipeline. Saudi authorities said on Friday drones launched from Iraq led to the temporary closure of a crucial oil export route used to bypass the lockdown of the Strait of Hormuz. Riyadh has increased its use of the East-West pipeline, which links Abqaiq, near the Gulf, to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, since the start of the Middle East war to bypass the closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran. The Saudi foreign ministry condemned “the targeting of the East–West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions by several drones coming from Iraq, which caused human injuries and damage”. “The pipeline was stopped as a precaution, and the attacks resulted in some injuries,” an energy ministry official told the SPA news agency earlier. Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Madina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline that carries Saudi oil to its Red Sea coast. The office of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi confirmed the attack originated from Iraqi territory and said on X that the commander in charge of the southern province of Maysan had been dismissed. The Iraqi government said it condemned “the attacks targeting our brethren in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia originated from a location within the governorate”. ‘Dangerous escalation’ Riyadh said that, at the Iraqi prime minister’s request, it had chosen “not to respond at this stage and to support the efforts of the Iraqi government … to prevent attacks launched from Iraq against the Kingdom and neighbouring countries”. Riyadh previously accused Iraqi militias of targeting its oil infrastructure. But it stressed that the kingdom “reserves the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, its security, its facilities,” and its people. Bahrain, Jordan and Qatar also condemned the attack on the Saudi pipeline, while the Gulf Cooperation Council denounced “a dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat to the security of the Kingdom”. Oil prices have climbed past $100 a barrel this week, while average US diesel prices topped $6 for the first time on Friday — a potential headache for President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections. Houthi rebels announced a maritime blockade in July against Saudi Arabia — which supports the Yemeni government — attacking its oil tankers in the Red Sea. By taking control of the Yemeni Red Sea coast and the islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Friday, the Houthis consolidated their grip on the strategic passage linking Europe and Asia. Navigation through the Bab el-Mandab Strait was “safe” for all but Saudi Arabia following the latest advances, the Houthis said.

Shafqat Ali Khan presents diplomatic credentials as Pakistan’s first envoy to Armenia. Shafqat Ali Khan, Pakistan’s first ambassador to Armenia, presented his letters of credence to President Vahagn Khachaturyan at a formal ceremony at the presidential palace, it emerged on Saturday. President Khachaturyan warmly welcomed Ambassador Khan, congratulated him on his appointment, and conveyed his best wishes for a successful tenure and the effective discharge of his diplomatic responsibilities. The president expressed his readiness to support efforts to further develop relationship between the countries and expand cooperation in areas of mutual interest. Ferdinandh CABRERA / AFP Report 358 / Asia-Pacific 03 September 2026 20+ minutes Policing the Bangsamoro: Peace in the Southern Philippines Security continues to be a concern in the autonomous region of Bangsamoro in the southern Philippines. Law enforcement reforms and better coordination between the military and the police – as well as stronger gun control and better access to courts – could help stem the violence. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Related Tags Philippines What’s new? Despite a 2014 peace agreement, crime and violence continue to rack the Bangsamoro region in the southern Philippines. The military, which is still in charge of public safety, as well as the police and an array of local institutions are wrestling with outbreaks of fighting powered by easy access to firearms. Why does it matter? Local conflicts persist across the Bangsamoro, and the implementation of key provisions of the 2014 peace agreement remains well behind schedule. Entrenched clan feuds, political violence and criminal rackets make it hard to foster the trust in state institutions and social bonds needed to withstand future conflict. What should be done? Reforms to make regional law enforcement stronger, more professional and responsive to community needs are vital, as well as better coordination between the military and the police. Access to courts, control over firearms, and reinforced peacebuilding are also imperative to prevent the escalation of local violence and tackle its roots. Executive Summary The 2014 peace accord ended decades of conflict between the Philippine government and Moro Muslim separatists in what is now the Bangsamoro autonomous region. But violence still flares as clan feuds, political rivalries and criminal rackets rattle the region. The police struggle to keep pace, leaving the military as the dominant security force. Other institutions remain ill prepared for the challenge. Courts are slow and often fail to guarantee justice, while institutions tasked with maintaining peace in the region have been afflicted by political infighting between factions of the former insurgent movement, and have yet to become fully operational. A clearer division of responsibility between Manila and regional authorities, along with a broader recognition of the roots of local conflict and the recurrent outbreaks of violence they cause, will be crucial to improving security conditions. At the heart of these efforts should be a reform of the police, bolstering recruitment, internal discipline and community policing. Tighter gun control, targeted justice reforms and peacebuilding initiatives should complement these efforts. After decades of war between the Philippine government and Moro rebels, progress toward curbing violence in the Bangsamoro region since it became autonomous in 2019 has been patchy. While the largest armed movement in the region, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), has renounced armed struggle and shifted its attention to the regional parliament and government, flare-ups of competitive political violence now outweigh rebel or militant fighting with the state. Clan feuds and electoral rivalries drive vendettas that regularly displace entire communities and weaken state authority. Criminal rackets are rife and firearms are easy to get hold of, fuelling cycles of violence. Key aspects of the 2014 peace agreement, including its security provisions, remain unfulfilled. This includes rebel disarmament, but also the redeployment of the military to other parts of the country and the disarmament of private militias. One of the biggest challenges in the normalisation process, as the region’s transition from war to peace is officially called, remains policing. The issue of who should be in charge of maintaining peace and order was the subject of intense debate during peace talks and in crafting the region’s autonomy law. Granting the regional government authority to handle public security was one option, but in the end Manila retained policing power in the region. Even so, the national police has struggled to define its role in areas of the newly autonomous region that remain affected by violence. Meanwhile, the integration of Moro ex‑rebels into the police force has been painstakingly slow. In the absence of a credible and capable police force in the region, the Philippine armed forces are still the dominant security institution in the Bangsamoro. In the absence of a credible and capable police force in the region, the Philippine armed forces are still the dominant security institution in the Bangsamoro. The military has earned public respect after decades of fighting a counterinsurgency in the area, but it is ill suited to handling local conflicts over the long run. Manila is grappling with how best to manage these dilemmas by continuing to deploy the military while using the police as backup. This approach, however, runs counter to the national government’s broader strategy of pivoting away from counterinsurgency to focus instead on external defence. For communities across the Bangsamoro hit by recurrent waves of violence, help is not always ready to hand. Communities often see the police as weaker, more politicised (especially due to local powerbrokers’ influence) and less dependable than the military. The regional government has greater powers over local dispute resolution and is in charge of building the local justice system, but is struggling to use its resources and is roiled by infighting. Long distances, case backlogs and steep costs mean local courts are often inaccessible to the Bangsamoro’s poorest citizens. The judiciary’s shortcomings are exacerbated by frequent score-settling between rival clans or bands, which can turn the filing of a legal case in court after a killing into the pretext for a fresh round of blood-letting and retaliation from the perpetrator’s clan. A rich tradition of community-based conflict resolution across the region offers alternatives, but its interaction with formal institutions has been uneven, and disputes often end up resurfacing. Both the national and regional governments should undertake reforms to mitigate violence and build a firmer foundation for handling threats to security. Supporting and professionalising the police is critical, but building a credible force will depend on practical improvements rather than sweeping reforms. Sustained efforts to rethink force structure, training and anti-corruption initiatives would help create a service responsive to the region’s needs. The police should also work to build better relations with communities, above all by addressing their most urgent concerns. Recruiting and training community safety police officers could be one way of bridging that gap. Ensuring better coordination between the military and police is also imperative. One solution would be for the military to gradually step back, enabling the police to take on more responsibilities for the management of public order. The relative calm in parts of the region should make this shift possible in at least some areas. These innovations should be accompanied by institutional reforms. The Bangsamoro needs sturdier mechanisms for settling disputes. Judicial reforms are also essential. For now, the formal justice system in the Bangsamoro remains weak, slow and too hard for its citizens to access, undermining public confidence in the courts. Strengthening Bangsamoro courts of all kinds with resources and personnel is paramount. Lastly, there are simply too many guns in the region for its citizens to be safe. Deterring gun use and clamping down on the supply of illegal weapons are essential to halt firearms proliferation. Together, these reforms should help curb the drivers of local violence, steer the region away from cycles of conflict and ensure law enforcement is in the hands of professional institutions that are responsive to the people of the Bangsamoro. Much as it was a singular achievement to end decades of insurgency, communities will not feel safe until the peace gets the policing it needs. Introduction For over five decades, a secessionist war raged in the Philippines’ southernmost island of Mindanao. The Muslim Moro people – who long experienced discrimination in the country – agitated for self-determination. 1 The term “Moro” refers to Islamised people in the southern Philippines, comprising thirteen ethno-linguistic groups. Two main armed movements representing Moro Muslim communities emerged: the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and its post 1977 splinter, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). 2 For earlier reporting on the peace process and transition, see Crisis Group Asia Reports N°355, Peace in the Philippines: The Bangsamoro’s Moment of Truth ; N°331, Southern Philippines: Making Peace Stick in the Bangsamoro , 1 May 2023; N°323, Islamist Militancy in the Southern Philippines , 18 March 2022; N°322, Southern Philippines: Fostering an Inclusive Bangsamoro , 18 February 2022; N°313, Southern Philippines: Keeping Normalisation on Track in the Bangsamoro , 15 April 2021; and N°306, Southern Philippines: Tackling Clan Politics in the Bangsamoro , 14 April 2020. The Philippine government deployed its military, paramilitary auxiliaries, and police against these groups. Over 120,000 people died in a conflict that did huge harm to public trust in state institutions and propagated the spread of weapons across numerous communities. The 2014 peace accord between Manila and the MILF – which provided political and fiscal autonomy to the Moro people within the boundaries of the Philippine state – marked a vital step toward reconciliation. In 2018, the Philippine Congress passed the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which voters then endorsed in a two-stage plebiscite in early 2019, thereby creating the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). The Bangsamoro Transition Authority, an interim government led by the MILF, assumed power that February. The interim authority exercises self-governance in the Bangsamoro region, home to more than four million people spread across five provinces. The peace agreement foresaw two parallel tracks to achieve full Bangsamoro autonomy. First, former rebels would run the interim regional administration, pass new laws and build institutions. This political track was meant to conclude with regional elections in 2022, but these have been postponed several times, and are now planned for September 2026. Secondly, a “normalisation” agenda was to guide the broader transition from war to peace; it includes issues such as rebel disarmament but also socio-economic development and policing in the region. 3 The normalisation process does not have a set deadline and instead relies on qualitative milestones; both sides are meant to sign an “Exit Agreement” after they have met their respective commitments. As with the political track, however, the normalisation process has fallen behind schedule. Achieving durable peace remains difficult in part because of deep social divisions. Achieving durable peace remains difficult in part because of deep social divisions. Kinship networks, entrenched political clans, diverse ethnolinguistic identities, and the uneasy coexistence of emerging political parties with armed movements all shape the region’s public life. Talking about his movement’s transition from guerrilla warfare to governance, a senior MILF commander admitted: “It was easier in the jungle”. 4 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. Political tensions have also flared within the former insurgency. In March 2025, Manila replaced the region’s chief minister, MILF Chairman Murad Ebrahim, with the organisation’s military chief, Abdulraof Macacua. This change fractured the movement, pitting commanders and cadres loyal to the Central Committee against Macacua’s faction. 5 Murad is closely aligned with MILF’s chief negotiator and head of its implementing panel Mohagher Iqbal, who wields substantial influence over the movement’s political cadres. In response to Macacua’s perceived violations of internal regulations, the Central Committee suspended both him and eight loyal senior commanders from their roles, stopping short of expelling them from the organisation. The Bangsamoro region governs itself – the interim government, for example, exercises control over public finances – but the state’s use of force remains under Manila’s control. Specifically, the national government retains command over the police, while the armed forces play an active role in ensuring security. This arrangement reflects the national government’s enduring caution about a region with a long history of rebellion and the Philippine constitution, which mandates just one police force. 6 Crisis Group interviews, Manila, 8 May 2026. See also Article XVI, Section 6 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution. Building on Crisis Group’s earlier work in the Bangsamoro, this report explores how public security is managed in the region, with particular attention to policing. It draws on years of field research in the Bangsamoro and Manila, including over 80 interviews with police and military officers, MILF commanders, representatives of the interim regional government, national and local officials, civil society figures, clan leaders, donors, villagers and decommissioned fighters. Women comprised around a third of interviewees. II. The Peace Deal and its Violent Aftermath Despite the undeniable progress made since the 2014 peace agreement, the Bangsamoro continues to grapple with security dilemmas. Although large-scale fighting has stopped, more than a third of young people across the region have experienced armed conflict within or near their homes since 2019. 7 Bangsamoro Youth Commission, “Bangsamoro Youth Assessment Study”, 2024, p. 60. A local civil society leader described the region as being in a state of “controlled peace”. 8 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. Navigating sporadic outbursts of disorder remains particularly challenging for law enforcement. A. Conflict and Crime The national government now faces two main security threats in Mindanao. Its first concern are jihadist groups that have stayed out of the peace process and continue to fight the state. With the regional government’s support, Manila has managed to subdue cells from these outfits in the Sulu archipelago and contain groups in Central Mindanao. 9 Crisis Group interview, MILF commander, Cotabato City, 2 November 2023. The regional government has several programs to support fighters who gave up arms, and the MILF also played a role in influencing young Moros to cease armed struggle. But while their attacks on security forces have declined, these groups have not been decimated. 10 On 14 December 2025, a shooting at Sydney’s Bondi Beach claimed the lives of fifteen people at the hands of father and son, Sajid and Naveed Akram. In the weeks leading up to the attack, the duo had spent several weeks in Davao City in eastern Mindanao. While some investigative journalists suggested the journey was an attempt to establish ties with local jihadist networks, their precise motives for the trip remain unconfirmed. Crisis Group phone interviews, December 2025. Some locals fear that former militants could re-emerge. 11 Crisis Group interview, member of a peacebuilding non-governmental organisation from Maguindanao del Sur, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Remnants of the nationwide communist insurgency, the New People’s Army, also operate in parts of the region, particularly Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte. 12 Crisis Group Report N°338, Calming the Long War in the Philippine Countryside , 19 April 2024. According to government statistics, the insurgency numbers less than 1,000 fighters and no longer has any large units combining political cadres and fighters. Manila has looked to the military to patrol areas where these waning insurgencies persist. Meanwhile, the police take the lead in handling law and order in calmer areas, where guerrilla presence is negligible. Another obstacle to durable peace revolves around violent disputes over land and politics that have long plagued the region. Some of those are clan feuds, known as rido , and others are communal conflicts. These types of conflict are collectively referred to as “horizontal violence” by journalists and academics. 13 Crisis Group interview, civil society activist, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Clan feuds are comparable to vendettas. The number of shootings, particularly in Central Mindanao (Cotabato City, Maguindanao del Sur and parts of Lanao del Sur), is such that one parliamentarian described the atmosphere as “pervasive lawlessness”. 14 Crisis Group interview, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 17 February 2026. A local conflict watchdog, using data from community networks, has recorded hundreds of incidents since January 2026 alone. See “Safeguard the Bangsamoro Vote: A critical period to transcend violence in the region”, Climate Conflict Action Asia, 30 July 2026. With many local disputes escalating into large-scale clashes, the failures of both the military and police to deter shootings have become conspicuous. The upcoming parliamentary elections are likely to aggravate tensions, as rival political blocs and local elites may enlist armed groups to intimidate voters or disturb the ballot. 15 Crisis Group interview, Bangsamoro political strategist, 28 April 2026, Manila. The three local elections held in the region since its creation – in 2022, 2024 and 2025 – were less volatile than in the past but still featured high levels of violence. Infighting within the MILF is also a source of tension. 16 Crisis Group interviews, community leaders and officials, Cotabato City, 5-6 August 2026. While certain disputes stem from local resource control, deepening rifts within the MILF drive other conflicts. Frequently, these dynamics intertwine as factionalism amplifies existing land conflicts. Crisis Group interview, conflict researcher, Manila, 13 August 2026. Violence escalates quickly and frequently recurs in the region’s most conflict-affected areas, with outbreaks occurring most recently in the Special Geographic Area and parts of Maguindanao del Sur. 17 An ambush on Bangsamoro’s Chief Minister Macacua in the village of Bitu in Maguindanao del Norte by unidentified gunmen further highlighted the region’s volatility. The attack did not hurt anyone in Macacua’s convoy. Edwin Fernandez, “BARMM chief survives ambush in Maguindanao”, Inquirer , 16 August 2026. Criminal activity in the Bangsamoro also thrives wherever state authority is weak. While petty crimes such as theft or robberies are relatively rare in the region, illicit economies are ubiquitous, and have evolved in parallel to the peace process. 18 Crisis Group interviews, observers and police officers, February-March 2026. Kidnappings for ransom, which used to be Mindanao’s most lucrative business, have almost disappeared; smuggling, however, has proliferated, including for goods ranging from weapons to cooking oil. 19 Maritime Bangsamoro in particular, especially the provinces of Tawi-Tawi and Basilan, along with its former province Sulu, has traditionally been Mindanao’s “backdoor”, where many local communities have long treated smuggling to and from the Malaysian state of Sabah as legitimate commerce. In Central Mindanao, illicit cigarette trading has also flourished, much of it supplied from Indonesia and Vietnam and allegedly shielded by local powerbrokers. Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026; diplomats, Manila, 30 April 2026. See also, United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, “ An Interconnected Criminal Ecosystem: Transnational Organized Crime Threat Assessment for South-East Asia ”, July 2026, pp. 216-217. This illicit activity, however, has not led to open violence between competing criminal interests as syndicates appear to work with local governments rather than against them, and turf wars are scarce. Human trafficking across the region, especially involving women, also remains a concern given the region’s porous borders and long coastlines. 20 See for example, Lean Bolongon, “Safeguarding minors: Combating illegal recruitment in BARMM”, Philippine Information Agency , 17 March 2026. Another profitable business in Mindanao is the drug trade. During former President Rodrigo Duterte’s term in office from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine police carried out a nation-wide anti-drug campaign that targeted suspected dealers and users, killing thousands. 21 Georgi Engelbrecht, “Philippines: The International Criminal Court Goes After Duterte’s Drug War”, 17 September 2021. While some Mindanao drug lords were killed, other networks survived and have since flourished. 22 Crisis Group interview, security analyst, Manila, 10 March 2026. As early as 2023 – just a year after Duterte left office – a local activist in Marawi declared that the “drugs are back”. 23 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 26 October 2023. The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency and the police continue counter-narcotic operations; some locals say they have recently seen an increase in arrests and shoot-outs. 24 Crisis Group has recorded at least ten such anti-drug operations across the region in 2026 so far. One clash in August between security forces and an armed drug trafficking outfit in Bongao town in Tawi-Tawi left one person dead and three others wounded, including a naval officer. 25 Edwin Fernandez, “PDEA agent, drug suspect killed; 3 Marines wounded in Tawi-Tawi”, Inquirer , 9 August 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power. The proliferation of firearms has also contributed to conflict and crime in the region. 26 It is notoriously hard to determine the total number of guns in the region. In late 2024, the police estimated that the region had over 27,000 unregistered firearms, while a well-informed interlocutor told Crisis Group that there were 20,000 legally registered ones. Crisis Group interview, 11 February 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power; decades of war have made weapons ubiquitous. 27 Individuals and clans carry a wide variety of weapons, ranging from antiquated rifles to machine guns. Other Philippine regions where guns are prevalent are Abra and Negros. Members of armed groups and many local politicians, civilians and ex-combatants carry these weapons. 28 The first armed movement in the region, the MNLF, despite having splintered into factions, also retains weapons. The 1996 peace agreement with the movement sidestepped the question of disarmament, but in the absence of any attacks on government forces by a MNLF faction since 2012, Manila tolerates the awkward status quo of hundreds of MNLF fighters still being under arms. Crisis Group interviews, MNLF political cadre, Cotabato City, 16 February 2026. Under the 2014 peace agreement, the MILF has taken part in the gradual demobilisation of its forces. In early 2026, however, the group stopped formally participating in the process and other normalisation activities such high-level meetings due to Manila’s perceived failure to fulfil promises of socio-economic benefits for combatants who lay down their arms; 14,000 fighters have still to be decommissioned, along with 2,450 weapons. 29 Taher Solaiman, “MILF declares ‘temporary pause’ in peace process engagement with national government”, Luwaran.com , 17 March 2026. Following discussions between its peace panel and government counterparts, the MILF ended the temporary suspension of its engagement in the peace process in early August, but demobilisation of rebels appears to still be on hold. 30 Carolyn Arguillas, “GPH-MILF Peace Implementing Panels finally meet; MILF’s ‘temporary pause’ lifted”, Mindanews , 5 August 2026. While there has been a proliferation of Philippine gun laws over the past five decades, they are strikingly permissive. Under a so-called Type 5 licence, for example, Filipinos are allowed to possess up to fifteen firearms. Existing ordinances, moreover, are loosely enforced. Individuals often acquire weapons legally but then remove their serial numbers, making them untraceable. 31 Crisis Group interview, police officer, Manila, 10 May 2026. Consequently, the government’s main focus is on the pool of “loose” firearms – those guns which the state cannot trace or document – with the goal of either seizing them or persuading politicians and civilians to turn them in. 32 The term “loose firearms” refers broadly to weapons that rebels, criminals or civilians hold without proper registration, including those purchased legally but later left unregistered or with expired licenses. But the task is overwhelming; civil society activists say guns continue to flow in and out of the Bangsamoro without any means to trace them. 33 Crisis Group phone interview, source from Basilan, 28 February 2026. High-calibre weapons such as mortars, machine guns or assault rifles can easily stoke local conflicts as their lethality increases the likelihood of casualties and tit-for-tat retaliation. 34 On 2 August, national police chief Jose Nartatez pushed for a crackdown on illegal firearms and armed groups in the region ahead of the September polls. Andrea Gregorio, “PNP ramps up ops vs gun-for-hire groups ahead of BARMM polls”, Inquirer , 2 August 2026. For its part, the interim regional government has only recently started discussing a bill to regulate firearms and ammunition in the autonomous region. 35 Member of parliament Omar Sema filed the bill on 16 April 2026, marking the sole instance that such legislation has been discussed in the regional parliament, out of the 469 bills it has passed so far. In the meantime, local governments such as the province of Basilan have launched programs to collect small arms and light weapons. This effort is being done in coordination with the national peace process office and is underwritten by foreign donors. Buy-in, however, has been uneven. 36 An obstacle to these schemes is that the market value of firearms often surpasses the cash incentives offered to rebels or civilians for surrendering them. Two senior military commanders expressed deep scepticism about the campaign, arguing that the initiative would have no meaningful impact on the security landscape, was far too modest in scale, and targeted the wrong weapons (those not in the hands of rebels or ex-combatants). Crisis Group interviews, Maguindanao and Cotabato, February-March 2026. Other proposed solutions, such as forced mass disarmament or the comprehensive registration of firearms, do not seem realistic in the Bangsamoro context. 37 Crisis Group interviews, interim government officials and civil society representatives, Cotabato City, February-March 2026. Efforts to create “zones of peace” or “gun-free zones”, often initiated by non-government organisations, have been short-lived. 38 Crisis Group interview, head of a civil society organisation, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. A checkpoint during the 2024 village polls in Lanao del Sur, Philippines. February 2024. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht B. Policing under Autonomy To meet the challenge of the post-conflict landscape, the drafters of the 2014 peace agreement had to think hard about the best way to police the region. 39 During the peace talks, policing was a key subject – as contentious as it was during negotiations between the government and the MNLF in 1996. That peace agreement contained no provisions for disarmament or demobilisation, and clashes continued to flare more than a decade after the deal. While the 1996 agreement envisaged integrating MNLF rebels into state forces, only a quarter of the insurgent force eventually joined the police or military, voluntarily bringing with them more than 4,000 firearms Crisis Group interview, military officer, Manila, 26 February 2026. See also, Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, “Integration of MNLF forces into the PNP and AFP: Integration without demobilization and disarmament”, unpublished paper for UP Center on Integrative and Development Studies project on the GRP-MNLF peace agreement, 2000. The agreement called for a regional police force that was to be “civilian in character, effective and efficient in law enforcement, fair and impartial, and accountable under the law for its actions”, and whose mandate would be “law enforcement and maintenance of peace and order” in the region. 40 Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro and Annex on Normalisation . But the division of labour between Manila, its national police force and the region remained ambiguous. 41 The Philippine National Police, created in 1991, is tasked with preventing and investigating criminal activities and strengthening internal security. The Department of Interior and Local Government has political control over the force, while the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) administers and disciplines it. The president selects the national police chief and senior police officers and appoints the secretary of the department of interior and local government. Headquartered in Manila, the force maintains regional, provincial and municipal stations across the archipelago, but also includes two specialised units: the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group focuses on organised crime and terrorism; the Special Action Force, the PNP’s elite commando unit, is in charge of counterterrorism, hostage rescue, and high-risk operations as well as ad hoc tasks such as patrolling hot spots during elections. One part of the agreement stipulated that the regional government, working in coordination with Manila, “shall have primary responsibility over public order and safety within the Bangsamoro”. 42 Annex on Power Sharing , Art. II, 14. In another part, the accord said the police force is “responsible both to the central government and the Bangsamoro government”. 43 Framework Agreement and Annex on Normalisation. The Philippine Constitution is clear in that regard, as Art. 10 Section 21 states: “The preservation of peace and order within the regions shall be the responsibility of the local police agencies which shall be organised, maintained, supervised, and utilised in accordance with applicable laws. The defence and security of the regions shall be the responsibility of the National Government”. Government officials involved in the negotiations say the agreement was clear the regional police would remain under national authority. 44 One official involved in the process, however, said that Manila dodged the hard questions until the end, keeping the wording intentionally vague, and ended up “parking” the issue for the future. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 31 July 2026. The MILF, however, maintains that the common understanding in talks was that policing should be under the control of the autonomous government. The agreement also set up an Independent Commission on Policing to determine how law enforcement should function in the new region. When the commission delivered its report in April 2014, it recommended that the force remain a part of the national police, but stressed that it should invest in community‑based policing. 45 The Independent Commission on Policing for the Bangsamoro, “Policing for the Bangsamoro”, 2014. Report on file with Crisis Group. Community policing is generally understood as an approach that builds active partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to solve community problems and jointly ensure public safety. The commission highlighted the need for community policing that respects human rights and Sharia law. Another problem the commission identified was the police’s weak accountability to the communities they serve. Tasked with translating the occasionally vague peace agreement into clear and legally binding terms, the 2019 autonomy law dismissed the idea of a separate Bangsamoro police force. Wary of clashing with the 1987 constitution’s centralised approach to policing, lawmakers assigned public order and safety to the national government. 46 A single national police force was mandated to curb the historical misuse of local law enforcement by warlords. Yet mindful of the authoritarian practices during Martial Law under Ferdinand Marcos, the constitution balanced this by granting local governments a supervisory role to ensure checks and balances. This outcome reflected the stance of former President Rodrigo Duterte, who was in office when the autonomy law came into force, but both the national police force and lawyers were also sceptical about proposals for a separate regional police force. 47 Crisis Group telephone interview, analyst, 18 February 2021. In early 2019, the national police established a Police Regional Office (PRO-BARMM), which is part of the national police and therefore firmly under Manila’s control. 48 According to most observers and local figures, any change to this status quo needs constitutional amendments. Crisis Group written communication, 12 June 2026. See also, Nash Maulana, “‘BARMM police, Moro Senate seat require Charter change”, Manila Standard , 3 May 2026. At the same time, the organic law included two compromise provisions. The first one was to allow the integration of MILF and MNLF members into PRO-BARMM (see Section III.A.2). 49 The MILF was critical towards integration of their forces into the police during the peace talks. Later, however, the movement accepted this provision in the autonomy law. The second one called for the chief of the regional police force to be appointed “upon consultation with the Chief Minister”. In practice, however, it is the national police chief who has ultimately decided on this appointment. 50 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 27 February 2026. In late 2025, however, a national police commission resolution reiterated that the region’s chief minister can both recommend candidates and provide feedback on shortlisted officers. III. Security and Justice in Transition Various bodies in the Bangsamoro region are responsible for tackling flare-ups of violence. While the police and military remain central to maintaining order, other government and community institutions also help dispense justice and mediate disputes. A. The Police during the Bangsamoro Transition As is the case with the national police as a whole, the Bangsamoro force is hierarchical in nature. Its regional headquarters are in Parang, from which it oversees five provincial headquarters and more than one hundred municipal police stations. Every town has a team of officers who mostly take care of basic law enforcement. These tasks include investigating crimes, preparing requests for warrants or subpoenas from the courts, dealing with minor offences and arresting criminals and insurgents. 51 Arrest powers remain outside the military’s purview, except in instances of “in flagrante delicto” where troops directly witness a crime. The number of officers in the region is, by many accounts, insufficient: a regular station typically has a staff of a bit over twenty, covering municipalities with populations as large as 25,000. Overall, the police force’s headcount stands at over 7,000. 52 Crisis Group interviews, police officers, Cotabato City and Parang, 6-7 August 2026. Every municipal police chief shapes the local force’s policies on everything from community engagement and collaboration with politicians to defining how to handle local conflicts. In the post-2019 transition period, the police has emphasised anti-drug operations and curbing the spread of illegal firearms. 53 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. These priorities stem from the national government’s priority of combating drugs, as well as community support for the campaign. 54 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Cotabato City, 6 August 2026. Given their limited numbers and lack of equipment, it has been more difficult for the police to address complex clan feuds, which can flare up without forewarning. In the most conflict-affected parts of Maguindanao, the police struggle to conduct even routine patrols, leaving law and order in the military’s hands. 55 A police chief from the region distinguished between “law enforcement”, for which the police is in the lead, and “combat operations” that are the domain of the military. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 17 February 2026. A senior police officer said the force can take care of so-called “soft targets”, but still need back-up if the operation occurs in a “harsh” context. 56 Crisis Group interview, Shariff Aguak, Maguindanao del Sur, 27 March 2026. According to one regional bureaucrat, the police may be willing to take over internal security but is currently “not capable” of doing so. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Perceptions of law enforcers vary. The police appear more connected to everyday life than the military because their stations are located near town halls, making them visibly present. Some officers have a genuine desire to help their communities. But for many young Moro men and women, becoming a police officer is more about acquiring a secure job than answering the call of duty. 57 Crisis Group interview, member of parliament, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 13 February 2026; academic, Marawi City, 27 March 2026. Some locals are also sceptical about the ability of the police to respond to incidents. 58 In Lanao del Sur, a civil society activist also observed the police are too slow to respond to violence. Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. Locals in predominantly non-Moro Indigenous communities also feel that law enforcement does not always respond to their concerns. 59 Crisis Group interview, phone interview, community leader, 6 December 2021; online communication, peace process observer, 17 August 2026. That said, several surveys show the police enjoy a degree of trust from local people. 60 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 20 March 2026. Surveys made available to Crisis Group. Other survey data suggests that many residents continue to look to local leaders and religious figures for security. Tatsuya Koyama, “Who Supports the Peace? A Survey of Postconflict Public Opinion in Maguindanao, the Philippines”, Journal of Current Southeast Asian Affairs , vol. 44 no. 3 (December 2025). At the beginning of the transition, many MILF commanders hoped community policing – namely, building partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to ensure public safety – would become widespread. 61 Crisis Group interview, senior MILF commander, Cotabato City, 27 November 2019. The Philippine police have used civilian auxiliaries known as the Barangay Peace Action Teams (BPATs) and Civilian Volunteer Organisations (CVOs) that came closest to community policing. With police approval, BPATs may carry light firearms. CVOs focus on intelligence gathering, neighbourhood patrols, and emergency response. Officially unarmed, they may use weapons when supporting police operations, although in practice some mayors or village heads have been known to issue them firearms. Despite the support of international donors, however, and its inclusion in the Philippine policing doctrine, this approach never really gained momentum. 62 Crisis Group interview, donor official, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Police officers admit that resource limitations, understaffing and local politics complicate the work of fostering stronger relations with Bangsamoro communities. 63 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato and Parang, 5-7 August 2026. Even so, some individual officers have been more proactive. A former police chief in Maguindanao, for example, instructed his officers to visit communities and engage residents on important concerns, at times accompanied by representatives from the judicial system. 64 This community outreach mostly relates to drugs and firearms use. Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. As for efforts to integrate MILF fighters into the police force, as stipulated in the autonomy law (see Section II.B), these have so far had limited success. In 2019, the government waived height, age, and education requirements for five years to allow more former MILF (and MNLF) rebels to qualify for recruitment in the regional force. After a two-year interruption due to the COVID-19 pandemic, 11,075 applicants took a special eligibility exam in May 2022, which 7,145 passed. Yet in the years that followed, the government earmarked only about 400 positions for the former fighters, and just 396 joined the police force. 65 At present, 36 women were considered for recruitment and have undergone on-the-job-training in police stations across the region. “The Peace Accords Matrix – Mindanao (PAM-M) and Civil Society Normalization Update Report (January-April 2026)”, University of Notre Dame, 3 August 2026, p. 11. While the interim government stepped in to fund their training, Manila subsequently grew sceptical of maintaining dedicated quotas for ex-rebels, and future applicants will have to compete within the general pool of all Filipinos vying for the 1,500 police positions available annually. 66 Third Party Monitoring Team, 9th public report, 5 May 2026, p. 61. A small concession was a resolution by the national police commission in July 2025, which extended the police application deadline for MILF and MNLF members to 8 June 2027. Bong Sarmiento, “MILF, MNLF members who want to become cops can apply until June 2027”, Inquirer , 17 July 2025. While they may not have joined in large numbers, the former MILF fighters now working as police officers appear to have integrated smoothly. While they may not have joined in large numbers, the former MILF fighters now working as police officers appear to have integrated smoothly. 67 Crisis Group interview, Manila, international observer, 21 October 2022. Police officers from Cotabato City said MILF recruits have been well‑received by their new colleagues, and a sense of camaraderie now animates the ranks. 68 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, 28 March 2026, 6 August 2026. The Third Party Monitoring Team – an independent body mandated with overseeing the peace process – has encouraged further recruitment, underlining it “could serve as a powerful symbol of previously warring entities working constructively to build a secure future together”. 69 Third Party Monitoring Team, 9th public report, 5 May 2026, p. 61. But prospects for further integration appear dim. Manila has demonstrated no appetite to reintroduce a quota for ex-rebels or hire Moro who passed the exam but were not incorporated into the force. A part of the MILF, furthermore, still expects the regional government to take over policing in the region in the long term. 70 Crisis Group interview, international observer, Manila, 14 October 2022. Crisis Group interviews, MILF officials, February-March 2026. In this sense, the policing issue is emblematic of a broader lack of agreement on the future of the peace process. 71 Crisis Group interviews, international and local observers, Cotabato and Manila, February-March 2026. Marking its new secretary’s first 100 days, the Philippine peace process office’s late-July report made no mention of policing. Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity, July 2026. A mural near the regional police headquarters in Parang, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht B. The Role of the Armed Forces While the region is immersed in a transition marked by ongoing episodes of violence, the superior operational capacity of the Armed Forces of the Philippines means that they remain in charge of most aspects of Bangsamoro security. In terms of force structure, the military has three infantry divisions across the region and two other divisions backing its northern and south-eastern flanks. 72 The 6th Infantry Division is in Awang, Maguindanao del Norte; the 1st Infantry Division in Pagadian, Zamboanga del Sur; the 11th Infantry Division in Jolo, Sulu; the 4th Infantry Division in Cagayan de Oro and the 10th Infantry Division in Davao City. Light infantry battalions are based in population centres, with companies deployed in key towns or villages. 73 A senior officer argued the military is the most visible manifestation of the state in some villages and enjoys more legitimacy than police, courts or local politicians due to better logistics, disaster response capabilities and ability to withstand clan capture. Crisis Group online communication, navy officer, 16 June 2026. Part of the military’s acceptability is also its commitment to the ceasefire with the MILF. To boost its reach, the military has also employed so-called force multipliers. These include paramilitary forces such as the Citizen Armed Force Geographical Units (CAFGUs). 74 President Corazon Aquino established CAFGUs in 1987 to help meet the challenges posed by communist and Moro insurgents. Aquino’s successor, Fidel Ramos, sought to scale back auxiliaries during the 1990s, but in 2001 President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, confronted with mounting internal threats, expanded their ranks once more. Since then, CAFGU contingents have steadily grown. The CAFGU Active Auxiliaries serve fifteen days a month and are integrated into the army’s chain of command; the Special CAFGU Active Auxiliaries operations also fall under the formal authority of the armed forces but local governments or private firms pay for them to guard businesses or secure territory. From the perspective of the military’s central command, maintaining these auxiliaries – which have tens of thousands of members – is more cost‑effective than expanding the regular force. 75 At least one government official told Crisis Group there is a cap now on CAFGU recruitment in Mindanao. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 27 February 2026. In some conversations with Crisis Group, however, commanders still pushed for CAFGU recruitment. Observers also noted recent training in areas such as Lanao. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 15 March 2026. Critics, however, express concern about lack of discipline, and say these paramilitaries are at risk of becoming private militias answerable to kinship networks or to whichever group pays them. They also get involved in local land disputes, either as direct party to the conflict or at the behest of landowners. 76 Crisis Group interviews, civil society activist, Marawi, 26 October 2023; MILF member, Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte, 28 March 2026. The military’s priorities in the region have shifted over the last seven years. The military’s priorities in the region have shifted over the last seven years. At the beginning of the transition, especially in areas where insurgent and militant activity was concentrated, the military focused on high-value targets and combat operations, leaving the maintenance of “local peace” to the police. 77 Crisis Group telephone interview, security analyst in Sulu, 24 August 2021. As the threat level associated with militant groups decreased, relations between local residents and military personnel have improved. 78 In the past, communities were fearful of the armed forces, but the Bangsamoro peace process has altered that perception, even if many locals do not forget the military’s past abuses and heavy‑handed operations in their areas. A key task for the army has since become that of “managing” the MILF: while waiting for the decommissioning of the ex-rebels, troops need to control the fall-out of internal feuds emanating from the movement’s involvement in local politics. 79 Officers try to keep community disputes in check by supporting conflict resolution, though there are variations in how they go about this. Crisis Group interviews, military officers, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 16 February 2026. Concern about rebel resurgence shapes military commanders’ threat perceptions, but from the division level down to the battalion, officers maintain fluid communication channels with their MILF counterparts. 80 Crisis Group interviews, military commanders, Lanao and Maguindanao, January-April 2026. The peace agreement foresaw the military redeploying outside the Bangsamoro, a move that military leadership should now be keener to make given the country’s shift of focus toward external defence. 81 See Crisis Group Asia Report N°349, Riding Unruly Waves: The Philippines’ Military Modernisation Effort , 12 August 2025. But beyond existing “rotational rationalisation”, which happens on a regular basis, military leaders have been cautious about reducing their footprint in the region. 82 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 26 February 2026. Redeploying the military was part of the peace agreement but has made only limited progress. For one thing, residual violence persists in Mindanao. 83 Crisis Group interview, foreign military adviser, Manila, 29 May 2026. There are fears that a sizeable withdrawal would leave a vacuum, with neither reserve forces nor police ready to step in. 84 A military assessment said that “apart from the intensified checkpoint operations, the police must proactively target criminals and private armed groups that may influence the election process”. Report made available to Crisis Group. A regional bureaucrat admitted that given the reach and intensity of local conflict, it would be good “to keep the military where it is”. 85 Crisis Group interview, bureaucrat, Cotabato City, 15 February 2026. There is a legal reason for the hesitation as well. Philippine law assigns the military primary authority over combating internal threats; for the police to assume control, these laws would have to be amended. 86 Crisis Group interviews, security officials, Manila, 4 February 2026. Examples include Republic Act No. 8551 of 1998, which restored the military’s primary role in suppressing insurgency and internal threats while assigning a supporting function to the police, and the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020, which gives surveillance and intelligence-gathering authority to both police and the armed forces. Members of the military – especially those in the army – also benefit from the current setup. Divisions and brigades wield not only military authority but also economic clout as they generate local jobs and may receive funds from local authorities. 87 Crisis Group interview, military officer, Manila, 22 June 2024. In addition, the armed forces’ current metrics for performance evaluation and promotion do not encourage a shift in priorities, with experience in counter-insurgency efforts still helping to boost officers’ career prospects. C. Law, Justice and Conflict Resolution The peace agreement and the autonomy law recognised that in order for the Bangsamoro to exercise self-governance, it will need a system of justice that reflects the region’s culture and values. The region’s citizens have various legal regimes to choose from. 88 Art. X of the Bangsamoro Organic Law . The regular Philippine judicial system functions through municipal and regional trial courts, ensuring access to common legal processes. These extend down to the community level, where the barangay or village justice system also provides a formal venue for resolving local disputes. 89 The barangay is the smallest unit of political administration in the Philippines, generally accounting for a cluster of villages. The village justice system, mandated by Philippine law since 1991, comprises local councils that are tasked with mediating disputes before they reach formal courts. Settling a dispute at the village level, however, does not guarantee it will not reignite. Crisis Group interview, Bangsamoro lawyer, Cotabato City, 5 August 2026. Moro and other Indigenous communities maintain their own justice practices. Rooted in custom rather than formal litigation, these systems remain outside direct government oversight yet enjoy the support of local people. Relying on individuals with no or minimal formal association with the state, these processes typically lead to amicable settlements. 90 Crisis Group phone interview, 17 August 2021. See also, Raihan A. Yusoph, “Hybridizing Justice: Cultural Legitimacy and the Limits of Traditional Dispute Resolution in Lanao del Sur, the Philippines”, Asian Journal of Peacebuilding , vol. 13 no. 2 (November 2025), pp. 207-230. Sharia, or Islamic law, also applies to Muslims in the region if they choose to submit to it.
