Under the supervision of the Philippine Supreme Court, several Sharia courts handle family matters and personal affairs, such as divorce or inheritance. 91 Ferdinand Marcos Sr. created Sharia courts in the Philippines in 1977 as a measure to curb the influence of the Moro rebellion in Mindanao. The peace agreement strengthened this type of jurisdiction. 92 While the MILF had originally envisioned a broader application of Sharia law, the autonomy law ensured the region’s jurisdiction did not extend beyond the Philippine constitution’s limits. Crisis Group interview, MILF official, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. Some local MILF authorities, such as community camps or commanders, also maintain their own Sharia jurisdictions. 93 The MILF officially pronounced its Sharia courts dissolved a few years ago, but the informal system still functions in some areas. Sometimes, communities perceive the Sharia courts’ actions as overreach. Crisis Group interview, local civil society activist, Cotabato City, 15 February 2026. But views differ across the Bangsamoro as to the desired scope of Islamic law. Many MILF cadres would welcome Sharia as the main legal system. 94 Crisis Group interview, senior MILF commander, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 26 October 2022. Some non-MILF members also think Sharia could “decongest” cases for Muslims in public courts, and strengthen the rule of law among Moro communities. 95 Crisis Group interview, 11 February, source from Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Other Moro Muslims, however, prefer the public court system, given that it is still the most official route and enforcement is at least formally guaranteed, over traditional mechanisms, which are perceived to be quick but less authoritative. 96 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 27 March 2026. Bangsamoro citizens use these different justice mechanisms – whether traditional mediation, Sharia or public courts – depending on the types of issues at hand, but also based on their class, gender or ethno-linguistic group. While in principle this “forum shopping” arrangement can be useful, problems arise if conflict parties such as former rebels, clans or insurgents fail to accept resolutions from these various judicial bodies, leading to disputes resurfacing and becoming more violent. [The] legal fragmentation makes Bangsamoro institutions offering routes to conflict resolution all the more important. This legal fragmentation makes Bangsamoro institutions offering routes to conflict resolution all the more important. The interim government has several bodies dealing with public safety, the most important of which is the Ministry for Public Order and Safety, whose mandate is to prevent and resolve clan feuds that have long destabilised the region. That said, the ministry’s small budget has left it with limited reach. 97 The Ministry for Public Order and Safety and some legislators have often channelled large sums to feuding clans as an inducement to settle. The ministry has also provided training to local community monitors. Initial hurdles at the outset of the transition, however, especially regarding the ministry’s precise mandate, and internal friction within the bureaucracy, have all hampered its effectiveness. Crisis Group interview, local analyst, 18 August 2026. In addition, as local conflict was rising around 2022, the chief minister created the Peace, Security and Reconciliation Office, whose mandate overlaps with the ministry but focuses more narrowly on disputes among MILF members. Leadership changes, however, have reduced the office’s effectiveness. 98 Crisis Group phone interview, analyst, 5 June 2026. Critics argue that the office’s impact has waned under the current director, Castro Emran, citing a perceived loyalty to the region’s chief minister over the MILF chairman, whose rival factions now compete with one another for political influence and mass support. More generally, many observers view him as less proactive in resolving issues than his predecessor, Anwar Alamada. Local government officials, meanwhile, constitute the first line of political authority, and are also crucial in dealing with outbreaks of conflict. They do this in two main ways. First, local mayors or village captains have the mandate to fix local disputes in their town or village. Secondly, they chair peace and order councils, which bring together officials, security personnel (including police chiefs and senior military commanders) and community representatives to coordinate responses when violence erupts. 99 Crisis Group interview, expert, M’lang, Cotabato province, 29 October 2023. Some councils meet regularly, thereby also playing a conflict prevention role, but others convene only after unrest has broken out. In many cases, the convening of the councils is a formality but does not make a dent on disputes. 100 Crisis Group interview, senior national security official, Manila, 25 March 2026. “They are often just talk shops”, quipped a military officer. 101 Crisis Group interview, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 28 March 2026. Finally, the peace agreement created Joint Peace and Security Teams – hybrid units comprising police, military and MILF personnel. While these are now deployed across 24 locations, they have limited mobility and only a few teams actually seek to manage conflicts. 102 Summary Report made available to Crisis Group, BARMM Peace Conference 2025, “From Consultation to Action – Advancing Peace Together”, p. 8. For instance, despite the presence of a team in parts of former Pikit town – a notorious conflict hotspot until a few years ago – a local noted that its effect on deterring violence or settling disputes is minimal. 103 Crisis Group interview, security manager of a non-governmental organisation, Cotabato City, 10 February 2026; local observer, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Some observers view their creation as purely symbolic – a confidence-building measure between Manila and the MILF, which is valued for their mere presence more than their real contribution. 104 Crisis Group interviews, local security analysts, Cotabato City, 9-10 February 2026. A local court building in Cotabato City, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht IV. Overcoming Community Insecurity Despite – or because of – a complex web of overlapping peacebuilding institutions, the Bangsamoro region is struggling to deliver the payoff autonomy was supposed to bring. Multiple actors – including the police, regional ministries, and municipal governments – help keep the peace. This system reflects a desire to prevent any one entity from becoming too dominant. But in practice this diffusion of authority means the underlying sources of conflict often go unaddressed. A. Law Enforcement Challenges Policing in the region is complicated by a thicket of operational challenges. As stated previously, communities in the BARMM require more police than current resources allow. The region’s geography, which includes porous coastlines, rugged and mountainous terrain, as well as isolated villages, further slows operations and inhibits deployment. With units overstretched, municipal forces struggle to deter clan feuds and must often wait for military reinforcements. In addition, equipment and training gaps persist, from forensic capacity to the absence of high power firearms or even patrol cars. 105 Crisis Group interview, policing expert, Manila, 12 May 2026. Locals also allege that, despite their mandate to safeguard lives and property, police officers tend to neglect investigating crimes unless citizens formally report them. 106 Crisis Group interviews, local community observers, Lanao and Maguindanao, February-March 2026. Finally, when feuds erupt in communities, police officers sometimes hesitate to respond because they fear they and their families could be dragged into the dispute. 107 Crisis Group interviews, military commander and community members, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. Allegations of corruption further undermine the police’s effectiveness. Theft or illicit sales of police weapons and ammunition has meant that on occasion arms meant for law enforcement have ended up in the hands of those it seeks to fight. 108 In 2018, for example, more than a thousand Kalashnikov AK‑47 rifles that the Philippine National Police issued found their way to communist insurgents, leading to graft and falsification charges against senior police officers. See also, Barbara Dacanay, “Manila: Top ranking policemen accused of selling high-powered firearms”, Gulf News , 15 September 2018. Anecdotal evidence indicates that some police force candidates effectively purchase their positions, and may look for more economic payoffs once in their posts. Observers also noted that the drug war under former President Duterte left its mark on the police, both in shaping the institution – heavy-handedness has become the norm – and through the practice of reassigning underperforming officers to Mindanao. 109 Crisis Group interview, security expert, Manila, 2 February 2026. Police officers that are well-trained and have a solid grasp of the region, on the other hand, are not always tapped for their expertise by commanders in the national force. 110 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 30 March 2026. Aligning law enforcement institutions with the peace process and ceasefires has proven far more challenging than it has with the military. Aligning law enforcement institutions with the peace process and ceasefires has proven far more challenging than it has with the military, which had more exposure to armed violence. This has resulted in several clashes between police and the MILF, as law enforcement officers failed to coordinate with the ex-rebels when conducting raids. More broadly, members of institutions such as the National Police Commission, and even senior police officers assigned to the region, especially when they are new, struggle to understand certain requirements of the peace process such as ceasefire protocols, largely because national authorities fail to properly explain to them why they matter. 111 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 27 February 2026. Perhaps the biggest issue concerns the national police’s accountability. In the Philippines, political influence on the police extends across all levels, encompassing provinces, cities, and municipalities alike. This happens because local officeholders, whether mayors or provincial governors, are automatically deputised as representatives on the National Police Commission, which supervises the work of the force. Political influence comes in two ways. First, governors and mayors play a key role in selecting officers for the positions of provincial or municipal police chief. Secondly, officials also have the power to direct and oversee the day-to-day functions of police in their area. 112 Philippine law, through Republic Act 6975, grants local chief executives “operational supervision and control” over police units, defined as the authority to direct, oversee, and inspect their operations. Mayors exercise considerable financial influence by providing essential equipment and operational funds that the central government fails to supply, often making the national police dependent on local government support. In the worst case, police officers even end up taking part in local politicians’ so-called private armies. Powerful figures hold different perspectives on how – or whether – to deal with political influence on the police. Some members of the MILF and the bureaucracy clearly wish the police would have no ties with local politicians, whereas political clans and local officials, unsurprisingly, are keen to preserve the status quo. 113 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, February-March 2026. Some military commanders Crisis Group spoke to also said that the police’s links to local politicians render the force “less effective”. 114 Crisis Group interview, commanders, Central Mindanao, February 2026. B. Fragmented and Politicised Institutions Another difficulty arises from the overlapping jurisdictions of the national government, the regional administration and local governments. Although the police and military are officially in charge of security, in practice the autonomous government – not to mention provincial and municipal authorities – often step in. This can result in all parties asserting responsibility, but only to the point they find convenient. For instance, even if regional guidelines on settling clan feuds are in place, personalities in localities where conflict erupts often matter more than institutions in curbing them. 115 Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. In addition, while the regional government has some prerogatives (see Section III.C), it does not stand above the security forces’ chain of command. To borrow the words of a local clan leader, all this means that the regional administration only has a “semblance” of authority. 116 Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 26 October 2022. Mayors, on the other hand, shift between resolving local issues when it works to their advantage or passing the buck to higher authorities or the military when it does not. Another concern is the interaction between the police and the military, which sometimes compete for authority, at times giving rise to a “power play”, as an observer who has worked with both institutions put it. 117 Crisis Group interview, Crisis Group, 11 February 2026. Intelligence sharing between the armed forces and the police, for instance, has proven difficult, and the lack of clarity in the division of labour between the two forces can blur accountability to the state and citizens if operations go wrong. 118 Crisis Group interview, former senior military intelligence officer, 20 March 2026. Intelligence sharing is particularly problematic when the target of an operation has relatives within the police force. The Joint Peace and Security Coordinating Center, a mechanism established in 2010, is tasked with coordinating military, police and coast guard operations across the country. At present, however, it mostly focuses on convening meetings and information exchanges. 119 The national police chief has acknowledged that “initiatives must translate to visible action on the ground”. Christopher Lloyd Caliwan, “PNP, AFP, PCG boost operational capabilities amid evolving threats”, Philippine News Agency, 6 March 2026. Although local conflicts are on the rise, no regional institution appears ready to grapple with the fault lines within communities. 120 Crisis Group interviews, former regional official, Cotabato City, 26 March 2006; civil society activist, Cotabato City, 7 August 2026. There is little incentive for peacebuilding in the Bangsamoro while the MILF Central Committee, regional officials aligned with Chief Minister Macacua and clans (who run local governments) are distracted by the push to outmanoeuvre one another politically and campaign for elections. Some bureaucrats, for their part, are also affected by the MILF schism and hesitate to advance peace initiatives, fearing their efforts will either be ignored or exploited by higher-ranking officials. In parts of Maguindanao, for instance, settling clan feuds often serves as a vehicle for powerbrokers to cultivate influence over MILF commanders, rather than a genuine effort to resolve disputes. 121 Crisis Group interviews, sources from Maguindanao, Cotabato City, 5 and 7 August 2026. C. Shortcomings of the Justice System A flawed justice system further undermines police effectiveness since it corrodes the rule of law and creates incentives for people to take the law into their own hands. Memories of decades of conflict, regular bursts of violence and communities’ past experiences with state authority make it difficult to make the rule of law more than “an abstract concept”. 122 Crisis Group interview, civil society leader, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Furthermore, the area is not immune to violence directed at members of the judiciary, either to scare them away or exact vengeance. 123 See for example, John Unson, “Maguindanao’s deputy provincial prosecutor, 2 companions hurt in ambush”, Philippine Star , 21 February 2020. High-profile incidents have become more scarce in recent years. Public perceptions of the justice system are shaped by its slow pace. Public courts struggle with chronic understaffing and backlogs. Judges sometimes postpone hearings because they are overloaded with cases, rotate in and out of the region, or cannot travel safely to remote municipalities. For ordinary residents, going to court is a costly ordeal, requiring time and resources many do not have. Public Sharia courts, often considered alternative venues for justice, also do not have enough judges, prosecutors and lawyers, leading to delays. 124 Crisis Group interview, MILF cadre, 12 February 2026. Sharia judges need to pass both the conventional bar and Sharia examinations. Some Islamic law students in Mindanao see this as a hindrance. MILF courts also often fail to live up to expectations. 125 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 10 December 2019; legal expert, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. A big obstacle to a well-functioning judiciary in the Bangsamoro is that powerful elites profit from a compromised system. A big obstacle to a well-functioning judiciary in the Bangsamoro is that powerful elites profit from a compromised system. A police officer observed that influential local elites at times encourage the force not to file cases against criminals, and that courts often dismiss the charges if local powerbrokers are involved. 126 Crisis Group interviews, Maguindanao del Norte, 26 March 2026. A well-off member of an influential clan, for example, said that despite his closeness to a prosecutor, the court is not likely to initiate action over the murder of one of his clan’s members given the perpetrator’s family is equally, if not more, influential. 127 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 28 April 2026. The weak rule of law can also perpetuate conflict. For example in murder cases, members of smaller clans face the dilemma of whether to file a legal case, which can result in retaliation from their opponents, or retaliate themselves, which could spark a cycle of vendettas. As a result, families sometimes choose revenge over a tedious and cumbersome legal process. In other words, the “culture of impunity” associated with the decades of conflict still exists. 128 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. A military officer with a long history in the region acknowledged that the justice system is “dysfunctional”. 129 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. D. A Stopgap Peace A major challenge to peace in the Bangsamoro is the fact that security forces remain unable to stem the horizontal violence that plagues the region. The problem persists in part because they tend to manage localised conflicts rather than resolve them, leaving space for violence to resurface. When clashes erupt, in some cases violence continues for hours before the military, which is typically the first responder, steps in. Beyond the physical dangers that communities face, these experiences undermine public perceptions of the armed forces, and more generally of what peace should entail. 130 Crisis Group interview, source from Lanao region, Manila, 8 May 2026. The military has tried to develop more flexible rules of engagement that allow for the immediate separation of warring parties, resorting to force if necessary. These guidelines, however, have not been applied consistently. Typically, the military manages to strike a ceasefire between the clashing parties, but as it does not have the mandate to resolve the issue that triggered the violence, the conflict often reignites further down the line. A vital element in these arrangements is often the payment of “blood money”, a form of compensation offered following an individual’s violent death. Some politicians, and even members of the MILF rank and file, have come to view this practice as harmful, since payment offers no guarantee that the conflict will cease. There are other obstacles to hammering out durable ceasefires. As conflicts tend to spill over village and town boundaries, a broader solution dealing with root causes in several municipalities, such as land ownership disputes, would be preferable. Municipal governments, however, often struggle to cooperate, which means this approach often is not feasible. 131 Crisis Group interview, former regional official, Cotabato City, 12 February 2026. In addition, regional ministries sometimes apply “ready made” solutions they have already successfully tested elsewhere, without taking into account the local context of the feud they are dealing with. 132 Crisis Group interview, MILF leaders, Maguindanao del Sur, 28 March 2026. This has occurred, for example, in Maguindanao. There were also cases where no ministerial intervention followed at all and local people resolved the conflict on their own. Even the MILF is not always able to resolve feuds beyond achieving a ceasefire. 133 In one case, a MILF commander around the MILF camp Abubakar hesitated to resolve a land issue between two of his followers and advised the village to take care of it. There was, however, no follow-up. Crisis Group interview, land experts, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Furthermore, a local non-governmental organisation noted that “infrequent and unstructured” peace dialogues most often fail to include women, young people with disabilities and non-Moro Indigenous people. 134 Moro Women Development and Cultural Center, Inc., “From Consultation to Action – Advancing Peace Together”, Summary Report, Peace Conference 2025, Davao City, 4 December 2025, p. 30. In some instances, this lack of inclusivity has perpetuated feuding or revived land conflicts that had otherwise been considered as resolved. V. Pathways to Local Stability Addressing the complexity of local conflict in the Bangsamoro cannot be done through a single sweeping reform. Rather, it requires a series of careful adjustments across institutions. 135 Crisis Group interviews, police, military and local Bangsamoro officials, January-March 2026. Focusing only on the police or the judiciary is unlikely to produce the desired results, which is why regional stability hinges on a combination of different policies. Police outpost in Cotabato City, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht A. Improving Security Coordination As the Bangsamoro stabilises, Manila has an opportunity to reorient its military toward external defence and set the foundation for the police to take the lead in managing day-to-day security in the region. While a full handover of responsibilities would be premature, the military and regional police can start formulating a plan to do so in the near future. 136 Crisis Group interview, police commission official, 12 February 2026. The existing Joint Peace and Security Coordinating Center (mentioned in Section IV.B) could be strengthened to take on this task. The centre should, for example, design more joint operations and establish a roadmap for regional and provincial security powers to be passed from the military to the police. Consolidating regional security will require a redistribution of state forces, while ensuring Mindanao retains a baseline military presence. 137 Crisis Group interviews, analysts, Manila, June-July 2024. The government should increase the police’s responsibilities in the region’s more stable areas, pairing this move with a gradual drawdown of military units. Mobile army platoons or detachments should deploy to volatile hotspots, including parts of Maguindanao del Sur, the mountainous corridor between Maguindanao and Lanao, and areas where non-Moro Indigenous communities live. To offset these small-unit redeployments, troops from the region’s flanks, such as the southern Visayas or eastern Mindanao, should shift to conflict-affected areas within the Bangsamoro in order to concentrate the military where it can maximise stability. Lastly, it is vital to deepen existing but modest military and police collaboration in Central Mindanao, through intelligence-sharing, joint training, and coordinated non-combat operations. 138 Crisis Group interview, senior military official, 16 February 2025. It is also crucial for the military to re-examine the rationale for auxiliary forces. In some areas that do not see conflict, some CAFGU paramilitary units should be demobilised. More broadly, better oversight of these forces is essential: commanders should apply strict accountability and disciplinary measures, and sanction transgressions. 139 Crisis Group interview, former military officer, Manila, 29 May 2024. In the long run, the Philippine government’s objective should be to dismantle all state-backed militias in a phased manner and rely only on professional forces. B. Reforming Regional Policing Reforming policing arrangements in a complex environment while remaining respectful of both the Philippine constitution and the Bangsamoro’s autonomous status will be difficult. As mentioned previously, Crisis Group takes the view that a Bangsamoro police force outside the realm of the national police is not practical at this stage. A more prudent approach in the short term is to reform the existing law enforcement set-up. 140 Crisis Group interviews, Lanao, Cotabato and Manila, February-March 2026. To that end, police stations must be resourced with the equipment they need. The national government should also hire more officers so as to boost the police-to-population ratio. Authorities could reassign qualified officers currently posted in peaceful areas outside the Bangsamoro to the region. They also could increase the recruitment of MILF and MNLF fighters into the regular police force, starting with those who passed the test but were never hired. Expanding the ranks of Moro officers would foster trust with both the MILF and with communities that still view the police with suspicion. Ensuring ex-rebel recruits receive proper training and mentoring, and are fully acquainted with the communities they serve, will be essential to prepare officers and cadets. Foreign donors involved with the peace process could support such initiatives with training design and funding. Adjustments in police operations could also help build a more credible force. Once it has the numbers and skills to do so effectively, the police should strengthen targeted deterrence in hotspots where clan feuds and community violence proliferate, combining surveillance, mediation and enforcement. It should also improve its intelligence gathering, including more information-sharing between police units and more efforts to question militants and individuals involved in feuding to understand the local drivers of conflict. Stepping up community policing would ... narrow the gap between police and the Bangsamoro public. Stepping up community policing would also narrow the gap between police and the Bangsamoro public. 141 Crisis Group interviews, police and regional government officials, Maguindanao and Lanao, February 2026. The regional police force should organise a new department that would recruit, train and deploy community safety officers. 142 Funding could come from the national or the regional budget, or a combination thereof. It should, however, bypass local governments and exclude their funding to prevent them from exerting undue influence. These would ideally be recruited among demobilised MILF rebels, and would be tasked with engaging local leaders and communities and conducting visible and non-confrontational patrols. They could also aid in criminal investigations. Before rolling this out across the Bangsamoro, Manila and the regional government could run a pilot project in some municipalities with independent monitoring of its progress. Here again, foreign donors could support such programs with targeted interventions. Lastly, to restore public trust, regional leaders should combat police corruption by enforcing existing regulations. The internal affairs service and other accountability bodies should reinforce such efforts through robust oversight. Tightening procurement and inventory controls is also essential to safeguard firearms and ammunition and prevent costly – and potentially dangerous – losses. C. Breaking Conflict Cycles Security reforms are vital, but quelling violence in the region will also require addressing longstanding conflicts. Regional and national authorities should strive to make local peace deals more durable and ensure stricter adherence to the rule of law. Curbing the proliferation of firearms will necessarily be part of that process. 1. Sustainable conflict resolution Tackling horizontal violence requires de-escalating tensions when they arise, preventing them from re-erupting, and addressing root causes through conflict resolution. To prevent local quarrels from morphing into full-blown firefights, security forces need to step in as early as possible. The army, police and MILF structures all have a role to play. While the military remains best equipped to quell firefights, particularly those involving clashing MILF (and possibly MNLF) factions, internal rifts within a single MILF unit are best mediated by the ex-rebels themselves. In case of minor incidents, relying on the mediation of trusted community figures would also help avoid escalation. Effective conflict resolution in the Bangsamoro should also reach beyond the rapid responses needed once violence breaks out to address the underlying causes of conflict. Initial ceasefire agreements should include clear protocols, including sanction mechanisms, laying out the next steps in case the conflict parties violate the terms of the agreement. Once ceasefires are in place, they require rigorous monitoring, whether through the deployment of nearby police and military units, or through the participation of informal community watchers – a mechanism that has already proved successful, for example last year in the case of some feuds in Datu Saudi Ampatuan and Mamasapano towns. 143 Crisis Group interviews, local mediators, Datu Saudi Ampatuan, Maguindanao del Sur, 28 March 2026. 2. Building inclusive justice The police may be the “first face of justice”, but the broader judicial sector needs to be reformed as well. 144 “Policing for the Bangsamoro”, op. cit., p. 18. A first task is to strengthen the courts. This should happen through better staffing and the provision of security guarantees for judges and prosecutors, particularly when it comes to accessing remote areas. Public Sharia courts also need more support, which could come in the form of training for MILF members who are currently judges in their respective communities, but wish to practice in public courts as counsellors. 145 Sharia counsellors are individuals who passed a Sharia legal exam administered by the Supreme Court. They can represent clients and practice law at public Sharia courts. Increasing the number of so-called “mobile courts” – whereby representatives of the judiciary visit far-flung areas where there are no tribunals – would also strengthen the standing of the judiciary. In the same spirit, the regional government should broaden access to the justice system for its most vulnerable citizens by subsidising legal fees and travel expenses for community members who need to go to court. 146 Crisis Group interview, legal official, Cotabato City, 5 August 2026. Encouraging state institutions to coordinate more closely with bodies engaging in customary practices such as community mediation would also increase the efficacy of the justice system. Courts and other institutions such as village justice systems can reap the benefit of these customary practices by formally recognising not just traditional mediators, but also the actual settlement agreements reached thanks to them. 3. Navigating the firearms conundrum Dealing with the proliferation of weapons is also imperative. To begin with, the government and the MILF should restart the decommissioning of firearms. Getting the MILF back onboard with this process requires the government to deliver the support it promised demobilised fighters in the 2014 peace accord. 147 The Annex on Normalisation stipulates that in exchange for disarmament, the national government will implement a variety of other measures including compensation for demobilised fighters and the economic development of MILF camps. Given the need for the government and the MILF to rebuild trust and overcome the current stalemate, a realistic timeline will require that the process continue after the September 2026 parliamentary elections. Beyond the MILF’s weapons, the government should address gun violence in Mindanao. That begins with getting a better picture of the number of firearms in circulation. In addition to credible estimates of guns in the hands of insurgents and ex-rebels, the military and police need updated inventories of firearms issued to police and military auxiliaries, as well as clear guidelines on the storage and safeguarding of their weapons so that leaks do not occur in the first place. The state should also disarm police or members of military auxiliaries who take part in conflicts or abuse their power, and dismiss them. For their part, national agencies must tighten controls on smuggling, imports and domestic manufacture of illegal guns, as well as strengthen oversight of gun licensing and weapon registration. Across all interventions, authorities should prioritise the confiscation of high-calibre firearms, given how lethal they can be. Deterring actual gun use is also critical. Establishing a highly visible and competent police presence should serve as the foundation for these efforts. To maximise impact, these police deployments ought to be combined with strict firearm bans across the region in the lead up to elections, when gun violence tends to peak. 148 The police said that until early August they arrested twelve persons for violating the gun ban. Joviland Rita, “PNP: 12 arrested for violating BARMM election gun ban”, GMA News , 3 August 2026. Authorities should also impose penalties not only on those who possess unlicensed firearms but also those who manufacture, store or use them for political ends. Religious leaders and clan elders can also contribute to eradicating the excesses of Bangsamoro’s gun culture by mounting campaigns to rectify the belief that the use of firearms beyond self-defence is legitimate. 149 Crisis Group interviews, local civil society, Cotabato and Marawi, February-March 2026. VI. Conclusion Armed rebellions have tailed off across the southern Philippines, but the peace they have given way to is constantly threatened by clan warfare, political volatility and factional disputes within the former insurgent MILF. The architects of the Bangsamoro peace agreement saw reforms to the police force, backed by improvements in institutions handling conflict resolution and justice, as a way to propel the region from war to peace. Yet a series of obstacles has slowed police reform and prevented institutions from maintaining law and order. Manila and the Bangsamoro government will need to work in tandem and be realistic about proposed reforms. A law enforcement system that is competent, representative and fair, and which can earn public trust by making communities safer, is an essential step forward. A more effective and accessible judicial system, as well as moves to tighten gun control and ensure that peacebuilding initiatives address the social and political undercurrent that lead to fighting, are also vital. These reforms would not only contain violence but also signal that the region’s institutions are catching up with its aspirations for peace. Somalia’s End-of-year Cliffhanger pzeiler Thu, 09/03/2026 - 16:47 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Podcast / Africa 03 September 2026 1 minutes Somalia’s End-of-year Cliffhanger This week on The Horn , Alan talks with Samira Gaid, founder and senior analyst at the Mogadishu-based think tank Balqiis, about the possible end of UNSOS, the UN logistics operation supporting African Union troops and Somali government forces fighting Al-Shabaab and what may come next. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Somalia In this episode of The Horn , Alan is joined by Samira Gaid, founder and senior analyst at the Mogadishu-based think tank Balqiis about the U.S. decision to oppose renewed United Nations logistical support for the 19-year-old African Union military mission in Somalia. Samira explains why UN logistical support has been critical to the AU mission as well as to Somali government forces fighting Al-Shabaab, and why its loss could leave some areas outside Mogadishu increasingly vulnerable. They also discuss what could happen if no solution or stopgap measure is found, and the 12,000-strong African Union mission ceases to function by the end of the year. They discuss how such a scenario could shift the balance of power on the battlefield between the federal government and Al-Shabaab. They also assess whether Mogadishu’s pursuit of bilateral security partnerships could fill the void left by a weakened or defunct AU mission. This episode is produced in partnership with the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung. Click here to listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify . For more, check out Balqiis’ report “ No Time to Drift: Somalia and the Deadline for a Managed Security Transition ” and our Somalia page. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/04/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 04 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Friday 4 September HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an oil tanker caught fire after the Houthis struck it near the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Jizan. The foreign ministry in Riyadh said Saudi Arabia would take all necessary measures to defend itself, while U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. would inflict “major military punishment” upon both the Houthis and their ally Iran if they attack shipping again. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says the risk of open hostilities, both in the Red Sea and along front lines in Yemen, is rising dramatically. 17 July 2026 CUBA Cuba’s power grid collapsed Tuesday for the third time in less than ten days and the sixth time so far in 2026. The island’s severe energy shortages began in January when the U.S. imposed an oil blockade, triggering a humanitarian crisis. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to bring about wholesale political and economic change in Cuba, as negotiations between the two countries stall. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the U.S. appears to be using civilian pain as a weapon in its effort to oust Cuba’s communist regime. Havana should pursue meaningful and much needed reforms, regardless of what the U.S. does. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. IRAN One month on, the 17 June memorandum of understanding that was to halt hostilities between the U.S. and Iran looks moribund. U.S. forces have been conducting near-daily strikes in Iran throughout the past week and resumed their blockade of Iranian shipping, while Iran has been firing drones and missiles at U.S. bases around the Gulf and in Jordan. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says that both sides remain nominally open to diplomacy. But the latest exchanges underscore a mutual willingness to use military escalation and economic disruption in gambits to strengthen positions at the negotiating table. LEBANON An Israeli airstrike Thursday killed two people in southern Lebanon, despite negotiations in Rome to end the conflict between Israel and Hizbollah. The latter rejects the Israeli-Lebanese talks, arguing that Lebanon should instead rely on the group’s patron, Iran, to secure a genuine ceasefire and Israeli troop withdrawal as part of a broader deal with the U.S. This position notwithstanding, Hizbollah has largely halted its own military operations in recent weeks. While Israel has reduced the intensity of its attacks, it persists in conducting lethal strikes in the south, where it continues to occupy territory. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the continued Israeli assaults undermine the historic direct diplomacy that is happening between Israeli and Lebanese officials. Left unchecked, Israel’s attacks could sour relations between Tehran and Washington even further, making it even more difficult to reverse the escalatory cycle that has taken off in the Gulf. 10 July 2026 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE UN Secretary-General António Guterres opened the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva Monday by reiterating a call for a ban on what are called Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems, arguing that “some decisions must remain forever human – none more than taking a human life”. Crisis Group expert Issandr El Amrani says it is urgent to regulate the use of AI in warfare: AI-aided weapon systems are enabling rapid processing of targets with decreased human oversight, with potentially grave consequences for civilians, as seen during Israel’s war in Gaza and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. These “killer robots” need not be fully autonomous to render human oversight largely meaningless. More than 120 states, mostly from the Global South, have endorsed such a ban. But countries that have this technology, including the U.S., the UK and Russia, oppose it, contending that current provisions under international humanitarian law are sufficient. CHINA China test-fired a long-range ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine in the South Pacific Monday, its first such exercise in these waters in two years. Beijing characterised the missile test as part of routine annual training that comports with international law, stressing that it was not directed at another country. Australia, Japan and New Zealand raised objections, however, with Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong calling the test “destabilising” for the Asia Pacific and Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara describing it as “a grave concern” for the world. Crisis Group expert William Yang says the test sends a signal to the U.S. and allies that Beijing is determined to push back against what it views as attempts to contain China’s rise. The test took place on the same day that Australia signed a mutual defence agreement with Fiji. It will likely push other Asia Pacific countries both to deepen such cooperation and to accelerate their own military modernisation. SOUTH SUDAN On Sunday, opposition fighters killed James Kueth Makuach, commissioner of Akobo county in Jonglei state, in what President Salva Kiir’s government described as an “assassination”. Makuach had belonged to the party of former Vice President Riek Machar, who was arrested on sedition charges last year amid fighting between his loyalists and government forces. In April, Makuach defected to Kiir’s camp. The president then reappointed him as county commissioner, breaching South Sudan’s 2018 peace accord, which allotted this post to Machar’s group. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the Akobo attack, which also took the lives of two other government officials, is part of an escalation in clashes in Jonglei over the past week. But it appears to have been an act of political retribution rather than a push for territory or another military objective. Makuach’s killing underscores the dangers of proceeding with national elections planned for December with no political consensus in Juba and swathes of the country embroiled in civil strife. 3 July 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan flared again this week. On Sunday, Pakistani forces once again carried out strikes across the border in Afghanistan, saying they killed 29 militants. Islamabad said the strikes were retaliation for recent attacks inside Pakistan, including a Karachi assault that killed three security personnel. According to the UN, at least 28 civilians were killed and another 49 injured in the strikes. Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban of sheltering anti-Pakistan militants, which Taliban officials deny. On Wednesday, Afghanistan said it carried out strikes inside Pakistan, targeting ISIS and other armed opposition groups. Islamabad denies Taliban accusations of harbouring such groups and noted that it had intercepted four drones launched from Afghan territory. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says outside mediators should push the sides toward practical border and security arrangements before the cycle of strikes and counterstrikes escalates further. NIGERIA Violence is again escalating in north-western Nigeria. Long plagued by bandits who engage in mass kidnappings for ransom, pillage and extortion, the region is also now seeing increased jihadist activity. Together, bandit and jihadist attacks killed over 150 people in Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto and Zamfara states in June, a notable uptick from previous months. On 28 May, Islamic State Sahel Province claimed what appears to be its first reported attacks in the region, in which eighteen soldiers and one police officer were killed in Kebbi and Sokoto states. Amid this escalation, on 20 June prominent bandit leader Bello Turji claimed responsibility for deadly attacks on troops and declared his group ready for either peace talks or prolonged war with the government. If the bandit and jihadist threats are not reined in, says Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi, north-western Nigeria could become part of the wider belt of instability in the Sahel. SUDAN Fighting centred on El Obeid, North Kordofan’s state capital, has intensified in recent weeks as drone strikes increase and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) mobilise around the city, raising fears of encirclement and blockade. UN relief chief Tom Fletcher warned Tuesday that El Obeid risks becoming “another El Fasher”, referring to North Darfur’s capital, which endured a prolonged siege before falling to the RSF last October and suffering mass atrocities. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says a siege of El Obeid would deepen the humanitarian crisis facing civilians, many of whom have already fled to the city from fighting elsewhere.
